headline: State desk: Curaleaf opens 82nd Florida store; NH home-grow odds
dek: Curaleaf opens its 82nd Florida dispensary in North Fort Myers on 24 November, and a New Hampshire sponsor says a patient home-grow bill will pass in 2027.
key_points: Curaleaf's North Fort Myers dispensary at 6350 Bayshore Road starts serving medical patients on 24 November, its 82nd in Florida and 192nd nationwide.
New Hampshire Rep. Wendy Thomas says her patient home-grow request, LSR 2027-0461, will pass both chambers in 2027 now that Democrats control the Legislature.
The bill would let patients and caregivers grow three mature plants, three immature plants and 12 seedlings; a 2025 version passed the House 328-42 before the Senate tabled it.
Gov. Kelly Ayotte is the main obstacle; Democrats hold 15 of 24 Senate seats, one short of the two-thirds needed to override a veto without Republican votes.
body: Two medical cannabis stories from the states this morning: Curaleaf keeps adding stores in Florida's medical-only market, and in New Hampshire the sponsor of a patient home-grow bill says the November election has changed its odds.

Curaleaf said on 23 November that its new dispensary in North Fort Myers, at 6350 Bayshore Road in Lee County, begins serving registered medical patients on Tuesday, 24 November. A grand opening follows on Friday 27 and Saturday 28 November. The store brings Curaleaf to 82 locations in Florida and 192 nationwide, according to the company's release.

The site sits on State Road 78 and, according to The Marijuana Herald, is meant to serve patients between North Fort Myers, Cape Coral and Interstate 75. It will open Monday to Saturday from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. and on Sundays from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., and stock the company's Reef, Dark Heart and FIND flower, Anthem pre-rolls and Select vaporizers. Chairman and CEO Boris Jordan said each new store is a way to serve patients who depend on it.

On our count, Florida holds about 43% of Curaleaf's US store base, 82 of 192. That concentration is the reason Florida policy matters so much to the company. Florida's market runs on vertical integration: each licensee grows, processes and sells its own product, so new stores are the main way to win share. As we reported on 19 November, Curaleaf, Verano and Trulieve all opened Florida stores ahead of the pre-Thanksgiving shopping rush.

The opening also lands days before DEA's 29 November supply-chain deadline for medical businesses with federal registrations or timely applications. For a vertically integrated operator that supplies only its own stores, the deadline is mainly a question of whether each site, from grow to counter, is registered or covered as a timely applicant.
> In Florida, store count is market share. Curaleaf's 82nd door is less about one town than about not ceding Lee County to a rival.
## New Hampshire: home grow after the election

New Hampshire is the only New England state without legal adult-use cannabis, and its patients still cannot grow their own. Rep. Wendy Thomas, a Democrat and a medical cannabis patient, told The Marijuana Herald she expects her home-grow bill to pass both chambers in 2027 and to sail through the House.

The bill is drafting request LSR 2027-0461, which we listed among seven New Hampshire cannabis requests on 22 November. Its text matches HB 53 from the 2025 session with only the dates changed. Qualifying patients and their designated caregivers could grow up to three mature plants, three immature plants and 12 seedlings, in secured locations reported to the state, with limits on visibility and access. It would also give home growers access to lab testing.

What has changed is the Legislature. HB 53 passed the House 328-42 in February 2025, but the Republican-led Senate voted 16-8 to table it that April. In the 3 November election Democrats won control of both chambers, including 15 of the 24 Senate seats and a supermajority in the 400-member House, according to the Herald.

The obstacle Thomas names is Governor Kelly Ayotte, a former attorney general whom she described as strongly opposed to cannabis. Thomas said public support, and whether Ayotte wants to be re-elected, will decide whether she signs.

The numbers show why a veto would not end the fight. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of each chamber. In the 24-member Senate that is 16 votes, so with 15 seats Democrats would need at least one Republican, assuming every senator votes. In the House, Democrats already have the two-thirds majority. There is a recent precedent: Ayotte vetoed SB 468 in June, a bill letting licensed dispensaries set up greenhouse cultivation, and the Legislature overrode her on 19 August, the Herald reported.

In Florida, watch Curaleaf's grand opening on 27 and 28 November and how the company and its rivals describe their DEA registration status after 29 November. In New Hampshire, watch for LSR 2027-0461 to receive a House bill number when the 2027 session opens, and for whether any Republican senator signals support before a floor vote.
